newsitem.title: INDONESIA: World body to promote tea in four countries.
newsitem.headline: World body to promote tea in four countries.

text.p: A programme to boost tea consumption in four countries will be launched next January by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), an industry official said on Thursday.

Moeljono Partosoedarso of the Indonesian Tea Association said the two-year long promotion drive would be launched in Indonesia, Slovakia, Zimbabwe and Spain by the FAO's Inter-Governmental Group on Tea.

"This has never happened before...where traders, consumers, exporters and producers participate to expand the market and consumption," he told Reuters, adding that Indonesia's East Java region had been picked for the project.

"Tea has been squeezed and is being squeezed by the giants of soft drinks. Compared to them, tea is nothing," he said. "The main objective is to increase consumption. The consequence will be increased employment."

Moeljono said tea consumption in Asia was lower than in Europe, with per capita consumption in Britain at 2.5 kgs a year compared with 700-800 grammes annually in India and a mere 200-250 grammes in Indonesia.

Industry sources said Indonesians consumed some 40,000 tonnes of tea a year, compared with about 120,000 tonnes of coffee. Indonesia is the world's largest producer of coffee after Brazil and Colombia, and ranks among the top five in tea output.
The program would entail affixing specially designed and patented logos on tea packets promoting the health benefits of tea.

Tea-marketers, producing countries such as Indonesia and the U.N.'s Common Fund for Commodities are providing the $4.6 million in funding for the promotion drive. The campaign will be run by the U.K. Tea Council, whose members include companies that market tea and producing countries.
The four countries involved would be considered test markets for the programme.
The industry sources said the promotion was a step in the right direction, but that it was too early to tell whether the project would be a success.

"The younger generation of Indonesians today are inclined to go for soft drinks because it is trendy, easily available and also due to huge advertising campaigns," one executive with a tea company said.

"East Java was chosen for the promotion because it is a tea-producing area where tea consumption is very low," he added. "Tea consumption in Indonesia is still relatively low, and I hope this project can boost its image and consumption."

The Indonesian Tea Association's Moeljono said Indonesia should take full advantage of the programme to boost tea consumption in the country, the fourth most populous in the world with more than 200 million people.
"Until now there has been no effort to promote tea consumption. What is happening is brand promotion," he said.
He said that like coffee, tea producers were also venturing into new products such as fruit-flavoured tea.
"The only snag has been that tea producers have been conservative in the promotion of tea because of the size of the industry and low prices," he added.
Moeljono said that on completion of the promotion project, he would propose that tea consuming and producing countries undertake joint promotion of tea.
